title: Aftermath: the missing money and the owner's suicide
summary: The commissioner offered the band work and got Hill out of town; the wife's mother and father also died, and McShann reasons the guitarist took the missing money.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: But really, back to all seriousness. He came back, he says, 'Oh, man,' Eddie was crying and carrying on. I said, 'First thing you got to do is cut that out. Now we got to start thinking.' So the commissioner of the town, he had a night club. So in about a half an hour, he showed up out there. So he says, 'Man, this is awful. Do you know, you guys liable to have all kinds of trouble. Tell you what you all got to do, you all come on over and go to work for me and you all get Eddie Hill out of town,' you know.
The word was out, huh?

The word was out. So that night, we says, 'Okay -- ' Her mother was over to the other big house, you know. When her mother found out what happened, her mother cut her own throat. Now, this is all that's happening. Her mother cut her throat and her dad was just coming in from Denver and when he come in and seen everything that happened, first, he was questioning about the money. He says, 'Who got the money?' He thought it was some Mexican fella got the money. He didn't like this Mexican guy. I never will forget this guy's name, the guy's name was Nestor. You know, he did not like this Mexican bartender.
He told me, 'Jay, I know Nestor got that money.' I
Well, the money was gone, was it?

The money was gone, but the reason I knew Nestor didn't get it, Nestor never showed up out there after he left that night, see? Nestor never showed. But I did know this guitar player, he kept telling me, he says, "Mack, let's go." I said, "Go where?" "Let's go to Oklahoma City." I said, "Man, I ain't got but $30 in the bank and I ain't going to --" in the post office -- and I says, "--and I ain't going to take that out and pay my way to Oklahoma City when I got a job to do on here. He says, "You don't have to pay your way. I'll pay it." And he's going to pay a couple of other guys' way. Then I knew where the money was. You know.

So the old man, he come over and sit and talk, says, "Well, who do you think got the money?" Well, this guitar player and a couple of other guys, they went on back. We stayed, see? So I just told him, "No, Nestor didn't get it. I'll stand all day and tell you, all night, that Nestor did not get that money." I says, "Now, the other guys, they're gone. But I know Nestor didn't do it."

So anyway, the old man, he told me, "I'm hurt. I'm hurt. I've never felt like this in my life," and so on and so on and the old man went in the bathroom and blew his brains out. I said, "Well, I done seen everything now." One,
two, three, four.
The woman, her husband, hermother and then did he commit suicide, the father?
The father, that was the last one.
What did he do?
Huh?
Did he shoot himself?
He told me, he said, 'I've never felt like this. I don't know what to do.' And so then we went on, started playing for this commissioner of Albuquerque --
Well, who 'we?'
It was Hunter Gray left, Henry Gray, Oscar Williams on drums. We had a great big guy named Homer Woods played the bass horn. He was an old-timer.
Well, what did Eddie Hill do?
Huh?
What did Eddie Hill do?
Well, we got the money from the commissioner and put him on the bus that first night and sent him on to Los Angeles, either Los Angeles -- somewhere in California, you know.
Is he still around?
I never did find out what ever happened to Eddie. He wrote one letter back there to us, said he got there okay, and I never heard anymore from Eddie since.
And the guitar player and a couple more, they went to Oklahoma City?
They went on back to Oklahoma City and I know that he's the one that got the money, the guitar player.
(Laughter.)
